newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China's crude oil imports to rise - analyst.
newsitem.headline: China's crude oil imports to rise - analyst.

text.p: China's net crude oil imports are expected to rise 28 percent in 1997 to 550,000 barrels per day from 430,000 bpd in 1996, a leading oil analyst said on Wednesday.
The crude demand is being generated by an expanding oil refining sector, Wu Kang, an oil analyst with the Honolulu-based think-tank, the East-West Center, told Reuters.
China, the world's sixth-largest oil producer, became a net crude importer in 1993 as explosive economic growth forced the country to turn to imports to meet growing demand.

Wu said China's gross crude oil exports will fall in 1997 to 350,000 bpd from 355,000 bpd while refining capacity would rise by 280,000 bpd. In 1996, capacity was 4.1 million bpd, although the utilization rate was just 70 percent, Wu said.
He said the added capacity would come mainly from China's first Sino-foreign oil joint venture refinery at Dalian in northeast China, which is expected to become fully operational next year.
The 100,000 bpd refinery, also known as Dalian West Pacific Petrochemical (WEPEC), is currently running at 80 percent capacity after starting up in October.
State oil refiner Sinopec also plans to add 50,000 bpd of refining output to its 110,000-bpd Lanzhou refinery in China's western Gansu province by 1997.
Wu said Sinopec's Tianjin refinery, near Beijing, was to be boosted to 80,000 bpd from the current 50,000 bpd.
An easing of bottlenecks at China's coastal refineries of Zhenghai and Moaming in the south was expected to add another 100,000 bpd.
Wu said demand for refined oil products in 1997 is expected to match the 1996 growth rate of 5.4 percent, but the refining expansion would offset any need to increase net imports of 410,000 bpd.
Chinese demand for oil products would be focused mainly on diesel fuel, which is used in transportation, to power agricultural machinery, and in shipping, Wu said.
While diesel is exported from the northern Chinese refineries to northeast Asia, it is imported in the exanding economies of China's southern provinces due to shortages there.
China's oil-product exports are expected to fall to 82,000 bpd from the current estimate of 85,000 bpd.
Wu said this figure would continue to fall in the years ahead.
He said the south still suffers from a lack of refining capacity and a poor transport infrastructure which meant moving oil products from the north to the south would be difficult.
